facts.statement: Rhamphinion is a genus of pterosaurs whose name means "beak nape" because the fossils come from the rear of the skull.
facts.quote: Rhamphinion (meaning "beak nape"; Greek rhamphos, "beak" is a common part of "rhamphorhynchoid" names, and the remains of this animal came from the rear of the skull, i.e. "nape" or inion) is a genus of pterosaurs from the Sinemurian-mid Pliensbachian-age Lower Jurassic Kayenta Formation of northeastern Arizona, United States.

facts.statement: Fossils of Rhamphinion were discovered in 1978 in Coconino County, northern Arizona, by an expedition led by Farish A. Jenkins Jr.
facts.quote: Fossils of Rhamphinion were first discovered in 1978 when an expedition conducted by the Museum of Comparative Zoology at Harvard University and the Museum of Northern Arizona led by Farish A. Jenkins Jr. collected several small pterosaur fossils from the sandstone deposits of the Kayenta Formation, dating to the Early Jurassic (188 mya -185 mya) in Coconino County, northern Arizona, USA.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen consists of fragmentary remains from a single individual, including two skull fragments, a possible jaw fragment, and an unidentifiable bone impression.
facts.quote: The fossils were fragmentary and all from one individual, consisting of two skull fragments (an occipital and partial jugal), a possible mandible fragment, and an unidentifiable bone impression.

facts.statement: Rhamphinion jenkinsi was described and named in 1984 by Kevin Padian based on the holotype specimen MNA.V.4500.
facts.quote: These fossils were described in 1984 by Kevin Padian, a professor from the University of California, who named a new genus and species of pterosaur, Rhamphinion jenkinsi, on the basis of MNA.V.4500.

facts.statement: Rhamphinion was once the oldest known pterosaur from the Western Hemisphere, a record now held by Caelestiventus.
facts.quote: At the time, it was the oldest known pterosaur specimen from the Western Hemisphere (now overtaken by Caelestiventus).

facts.statement: In its original description, Kevin Padian did not assign Rhamphinion to a specific family but suggested it might be a basal pterosaur based on its jugal bone.
facts.quote: Kevin Padian did not assign it to any family or suborder within Pterosauria, in his original description, but did note that the jugal was unlike that of pterodactyloids, and so may have belonged to a "rhamphorhynchoid", i.e. a basal pterosaur.

facts.statement: While Peter Wellnhofer considered Rhamphinion likely to be a rhamphorhynchoid, David Unwin classified it as a possibly valid species with uncertain relationships.
facts.quote: Peter Wellnhofer agreed that a "rhamphorhynchoid" identity was very likely, but David Unwin was more hesitant to classify its fragmentary remains in The Pterosaurs: From Deep Time, noting it only as a "possibly valid species of uncertain relationships."

facts.statement: Rhamphinion lived during the Sinemurian to mid-Pliensbachian stages of the Early Jurassic in the Kayenta Formation of northeastern Arizona.
facts.quote: Rhamphinion (meaning "beak nape"; Greek rhamphos, "beak" is a common part of "rhamphorhynchoid" names, and the remains of this animal came from the rear of the skull, i.e. "nape" or inion) is a genus of pterosaurs from the Sinemurian-mid Pliensbachian-age Lower Jurassic Kayenta Formation of northeastern Arizona, United States.

facts.statement: Rhamphinion lived between 199.5 and 184.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Sinemurian to Pliensbachian (199.5 to 184.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: Kevin Padian noted that the jugal bone of Rhamphinion differed from pterodactyloids, suggesting it might belong to a basal pterosaur group called rhamphorhynchoids.
facts.quote: Padian no lo asignó a ninguna familia o suborden dentro de Pterosauria, pero notó que el yugal era distinto al de los pterodactiloides, y por lo tanto pudo haber pertenecido a un "ranforrincoide", es decir a un pterosaurio basal.

facts.statement: Peter Wellnhofer agreed that Rhamphinion was likely a rhamphorhynchoid, whereas David Unwin remained hesitant, calling it a possibly valid species with uncertain relationships.
facts.quote: Peter Wellnhofer concordó que una identidad como un "ranforrincoide" era muy probable, pero David Unwin fue más vacilante al clasificar a estos restos fragmentarios en su libro The Pterosaurs: From Deep Time, notando que sólo son una "especie posiblemente válida de relaciones inciertas."
